## Instructions

Test your understanding of t-tests, p-values, and the logic of hypothesis testing. These concepts form the foundation of inferential statistics in psychology research.

---

## Part 1: Conceptual Questions

### Question 1: The Logic of Hypothesis Testing

We test the null hypothesis (H0) because:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The null hypothesis is what we want to prove</option><option value='answer'>We can calculate the probability of our data if the null were true</option><option value=''>The null hypothesis is always correct</option><option value=''>It is easier than testing the alternative hypothesis</option></select>

The null hypothesis typically states:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>There is a significant effect</option><option value='answer'>There is no effect or no difference</option><option value=''>Our prediction is correct</option><option value=''>The sample is representative</option></select>

### Question 2: What is a p-Value?

A p-value tells us:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The probability that the null hypothesis is true</option><option value=''>The probability that our hypothesis is correct</option><option value='answer'>The probability of obtaining results this extreme (or more) if the null hypothesis were true</option><option value=''>The size of the effect</option></select>

A p-value of .03 means:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true</option><option value='answer'>There is a 3% probability of getting these results if there were no real effect</option><option value=''>3% of participants showed the effect</option><option value=''>The effect is 3%</option></select>

### Question 3: Statistical Significance

The conventional alpha level in psychology is:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>.01</option><option value='answer'>.05</option><option value=''>.10</option><option value=''>.50</option></select>

We reject the null hypothesis when:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>p > .05</option><option value='answer'>p < .05</option><option value=''>p = .05 exactly</option><option value=''>The effect size is large</option></select>

A result with p = .07 is:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Statistically significant</option><option value='answer'>Not statistically significant at alpha = .05</option><option value=''>Definitely not a real effect</option><option value=''>A large effect</option></select>

### Question 4: Types of t-Tests

An independent samples t-test is used when:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The same participants are measured twice</option><option value='answer'>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>We are measuring a correlation</option><option value=''>Data are not normally distributed</option></select>

A paired samples t-test is used when:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>The same participants are measured twice (or matched pairs)</option><option value=''>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>We have three or more groups</option><option value=''>Variables are categorical</option></select>

### Question 5: One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Tests

A one-tailed hypothesis:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Tests for any difference</option><option value='answer'>Predicts a specific direction of effect</option><option value=''>Is always more powerful</option><option value=''>Should never be used</option></select>

A two-tailed hypothesis:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Is weaker than one-tailed</option><option value='answer'>Tests for a difference in either direction</option><option value=''>Requires a larger sample</option><option value=''>Is inappropriate for t-tests</option></select>

When should you use a one-tailed test?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>When you want a significant result</option><option value='answer'>When theory strongly predicts a specific direction and the opposite would be meaningless</option><option value=''>Always</option><option value=''>Never</option></select>

### Question 6: t-Test Assumptions

Which assumption applies to both independent and paired t-tests?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Equal group sizes</option><option value='answer'>Data should be approximately normally distributed</option><option value=''>Perfect random sampling</option><option value=''>Correlation between conditions</option></select>

The independent t-test also assumes:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Same participants in both groups</option><option value='answer'>Homogeneity of variance (similar SDs in both groups)</option><option value=''>Exactly equal means</option><option value=''>Large effect sizes</option></select>

---

## Part 2: Interpretation Questions

### Question 7: Reading t-Test Output

A t-test output shows: t(38) = 2.45, p = .019

The degrees of freedom are: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>2.45</option><option value='answer'>38</option><option value=''>.019</option><option value=''>Cannot tell</option></select>

Is this result significant at alpha = .05? <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

The number in parentheses (38) indicates: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Sample size</option><option value='answer'>Degrees of freedom</option><option value=''>Effect size</option><option value=''>Group size</option></select>

### Question 8: Interpreting Direction

Results show: t(28) = -3.21, p = .003

The negative t-value indicates:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The result is not significant</option><option value=''>An error in calculation</option><option value='answer'>The second mean was higher than the first</option><option value=''>The effect size is negative</option></select>

This result is: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Not significant</option><option value='answer'>Statistically significant</option><option value=''>Inconclusive</option><option value=''>Invalid</option></select>

### Question 9: Effect Size with t-Tests

Cohen's d is reported alongside t-tests to indicate:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Whether the result is significant</option><option value='answer'>The magnitude of the difference in standard deviation units</option><option value=''>The probability of the null hypothesis</option><option value=''>The reliability of the measure</option></select>

If t(40) = 2.10, p = .042, d = 0.65, the effect size is:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Small</option><option value='answer'>Medium</option><option value=''>Large</option><option value=''>Not significant</option></select>

### Question 10: Degrees of Freedom

For an independent t-test with 25 participants per group (50 total), df =

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>50</option><option value='answer'>48</option><option value=''>25</option><option value=''>49</option></select>

For a paired t-test with 30 participants, df =

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>30</option><option value='answer'>29</option><option value=''>28</option><option value=''>60</option></select>

---

## Part 3: Application Questions

### Question 11: Choosing the Right Test

**Scenario A:** A researcher compares test anxiety between students who received study skills training versus a control group (different students in each condition).

Appropriate test: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Independent samples t-test</option><option value=''>Paired samples t-test</option><option value=''>Pearson's correlation</option><option value=''>Chi-square</option></select>

**Scenario B:** A researcher measures depression scores before and after a therapy intervention in the same patients.

Appropriate test: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Independent samples t-test</option><option value='answer'>Paired samples t-test</option><option value=''>Pearson's correlation</option><option value=''>One-sample t-test</option></select>

**Scenario C:** A researcher compares reaction times between morning people and evening people (different participants).

Appropriate test: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Independent samples t-test</option><option value=''>Paired samples t-test</option><option value=''>One-sample t-test</option><option value=''>Correlation</option></select>

### Question 12: Formulating Hypotheses

A researcher predicts that caffeine will improve alertness.

One-tailed hypothesis: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Caffeine will affect alertness</option><option value='answer'>Participants who consume caffeine will have higher alertness than those who do not</option><option value=''>There is no effect of caffeine</option><option value=''>Alertness varies</option></select>

Two-tailed hypothesis: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>There will be a difference in alertness between caffeine and no-caffeine conditions</option><option value=''>Caffeine increases alertness</option><option value=''>Caffeine decreases alertness</option><option value=''>Caffeine has no effect</option></select>

Null hypothesis: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Caffeine improves alertness</option><option value='answer'>There is no difference in alertness between conditions</option><option value=''>Caffeine affects alertness somehow</option><option value=''>The sample is biased</option></select>

### Question 13: Interpreting Non-Significant Results

A study finds: t(48) = 1.45, p = .154, d = 0.41

Is this statistically significant at alpha = .05? <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

Does p = .154 prove the null hypothesis is true? <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

The effect size (d = 0.41) suggests:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>No effect at all</option><option value='answer'>A small-to-medium effect that may warrant further investigation</option><option value=''>Proof that the treatment works</option><option value=''>The study was flawed</option></select>

### Investigation 2

A researcher examines whether mood changes after watching a sad film. 25 participants rate their mood before and after watching the film.

1. **Design type:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Between-subjects</option><option value='answer'>Within-subjects</option><option value=''>Correlational</option><option value=''>Case study</option></select>

2. **IV:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Time (before vs after film)</option><option value=''>Mood rating</option><option value=''>Film content</option><option value=''>No IV</option></select>

3. **DV:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Time point</option><option value='answer'>Mood rating</option><option value=''>Film preference</option><option value=''>Participant enjoyment</option></select>

4. **Appropriate test:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Independent t-test</option><option value='answer'>Paired t-test</option><option value=''>Correlation</option><option value=''>ANOVA</option></select>

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The result is not significant</option><option value='answer'>Mood decreased after the film</option><option value=''>An error occurred</option><option value=''>Mood increased</option></select>

6. **Conclusion:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Mood was significantly lower after watching the sad film, large effect</option><option value=''>No change in mood</option><option value=''>The study was underpowered</option><option value=''>Mood improved</option></select>

:::

### Investigation 3

A researcher compares stress levels between employees who work from home versus in the office. 30 work-from-home employees and 30 office employees complete a stress questionnaire.

1. **Design type:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Between-subjects</option><option value=''>Within-subjects</option><option value=''>Repeated measures</option><option value=''>Correlational</option></select>

2. **IV:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Work location (home vs office)</option><option value=''>Stress level</option><option value=''>Employee satisfaction</option><option value=''>No IV</option></select>

5. **Results: t(58) = 1.89, p = .064, d = 0.49. Is this significant at alpha = .05?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

6. **The effect size suggests:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>No effect</option><option value='answer'>A medium effect that may be worth investigating with more power</option><option value=''>A large, meaningful effect</option><option value=''>The hypothesis was wrong</option></select>

---

## Summary Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- [ ] Explain the logic of null hypothesis significance testing
- [ ] Correctly interpret p-values (NOT as the probability the null is true)
- [ ] Distinguish between independent and paired t-tests
- [ ] Choose the appropriate t-test for different designs
- [ ] Interpret t-test output including degrees of freedom
- [ ] Write one-tailed and two-tailed hypotheses
- [ ] Understand what non-significant results do and do not tell us
- [ ] Report t-test results in APA format

::: {.callout-important}
## Common Misconception
A p-value is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is the probability of obtaining your results (or more extreme) IF the null hypothesis were true. This distinction is crucial for correctly interpreting statistical tests.
:::
